title: Chapter 94 — Goals, Standards & The Self-Managed Career
intro: The goal architecture, standards as identity, and the manager partnership.

sections.title: Goal Architecture
sections.content:
Set three levels of goals. The baseline: the minimum acceptable performance. Below this, something is wrong and you need to diagnose it. The target: what you are aiming for with consistent effort. This should stretch you but be achievable. The reach: what happens when everything clicks. This is aspirational but grounded in math.

Work backwards from the annual target. If you want $120,000 in income and your commission rate averages 18 percent of gross profit, you need to generate approximately $667,000 in gross profit. At 27 percent average margin, that is approximately $2.5 million in revenue. Divided by 12 months, that is roughly $208,000 per month. At a $2,200 average ticket, that is 95 sales per month or about 4-5 per selling day.

Now you know what your daily activity needs to look like. Goals without math are wishes.

sections.title: Standards as Identity
sections.content:
A goal is something you try to hit. A standard is something you refuse to go below. The difference is identity.

'I will try to make my Daily Five calls' is a goal. 'I make my Daily Five calls every day — that is who I am' is a standard. Standards do not require motivation. They require commitment. You do not skip them on a bad day. You do not negotiate with yourself.

Build five non-negotiable standards and defend them every day. Over a year, those five standards will do more for your career than any seminar, book, or motivational speech.

sections.title: The Manager Partnership
sections.content:
Your manager is not your boss in the way most people think. Your manager is a resource. They have coaching, floor authority, pricing flexibility, and experience that you can leverage.

The best rep-manager relationships are partnerships. You bring the activity, the customer relationships, and the floor skills. They bring the coaching, the T.O. ability, and the operational support.

Ask for feedback. Ask for observations. Ask them to watch your next up and give you one thing to work on. The rep who actively seeks coaching improves faster than the one who waits for it.
